set.approach: Start at the Stanley Glacier trailhead on Highway 93 South in Kootenay National Park and follow the signed switchbacking trail up through the trees until it opens into the upper valley, with the headwall rising on the right. Skis or snowshoes are usual in winter. The approach slope and the terrain above the climbs are avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast before going. The line starts to the right of Nightmare on Wolf Street, up the right-hand side of the headwall; reach it by the snow ledge that crosses the lower right of the face, which is itself exposed to avalanches.

review.notes: Approach: area trail and sector avalanche notes; route page for position relative to Nightmare. No descent stated.

set.approach: Start at the Stanley Glacier trailhead on Highway 93 South in Kootenay National Park and follow the signed switchbacking trail up through the trees until it opens into the upper valley, with the headwall rising on the right. Skis or snowshoes are usual in winter. The approach slope and the terrain above the climbs are avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast before going. This is the icefall at the far right end of the wall. From the trees the approach trends up and right to a broad snow ledge that crosses the face; this ledge is under extreme avalanche hazard, and some bolts along it can be used as running belays. A direct line up the big slope below the climb is the other option and is exposed to whatever releases above.

review.notes: Descent and ledge from route page; approach options from sector page.

set.descent_text: Rappel the route from the bolted stations placed after the first and second pitches. On the top ice pitch a v-thread serves as the rappel anchor, or when the ice is absent you rappel from the top of that pitch.

set.approach: Start at the Stanley Glacier trailhead on Highway 93 South in Kootenay National Park and follow the signed switchbacking trail up through the trees until it opens into the upper valley, with the headwall rising on the right. Skis or snowshoes are usual in winter. The approach slope and the terrain above the climbs are avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast before going. Nemesis is the farthest route up the valley, at the back of the headwall, beyond Suffer Machine, and is hard to miss.
set.descent_text: Rappel the route. Alternatively, rappel from a v-thread on the climber's left at the top to bolted anchors at the far left end of the mid-height ledge, then make one more rappel to the ground. With 70 m ropes the whole descent goes in two rappels.

review.notes: Two rappels on 70 m ropes agreed by route page and the Gripped article; v-thread/ledge anchors from route page. Approach from area page, avalanche atlas and Gripped.

set.approach: Start at the Stanley Glacier trailhead on Highway 93 South in Kootenay National Park and follow the signed switchbacking trail up through the trees until it opens into the upper valley, with the headwall rising on the right. Skis or snowshoes are usual in winter. The approach slope and the terrain above the climbs are avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast before going. The line rises from the left part of the broad snow ledge that cuts across the bottom right of the wall. Above the switchbacks and before the creek crossing, head for the right shoulder of the wall; there may be no trail, with downed trees, steep ground and cliff bands, and the way ends at a cave in the wall's right-hand part. From the cave, traverse the snow ledge, which can avalanche, to below the route; bolts are placed along it.
set.descent_text: From the top, rappel from a v-thread to the bolted station above the third pitch, then down the route from station to station to the ground, using long ropes.

review.notes: Descent and approach from route page (single source), no counts used.

set.approach: Start at the Stanley Glacier trailhead on Highway 93 South in Kootenay National Park and follow the signed switchbacking trail up through the trees until it opens into the upper valley, with the headwall rising on the right. Skis or snowshoes are usual in winter. The approach slope and the terrain above the climbs are avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast before going. The start is immediately left of Nightmare on Wolf Street. Reach it by crossing the avalanche-prone snow ledge that runs across the lower face; many parties skip the lower rock band and begin higher.
set.descent_text: Rappel the route from station to station, passing the bolted Nightmare station on the big snow ledge. Use a long rope; the longest rappel is the one onto that ledge.

set.approach: Triangle Peak stands across the North Saskatchewan River from the David Thompson Highway (Highway 11). Park on the roadside, cross the river by whatever way is safe, and bushwhack straight up toward the north face. Triangle Falls is the right-hand of the two obvious ice flows at the foot of the north face, with The Splotch on its left. Check the avalanche forecast, and treat the river crossing seriously because the ice over the river can be open.

review.notes: Approach from route page and area page (agree); no descent stated.

set.approach: The face is high on the cliffs across the river from the road, near Thompson Creek, and visible from the highway. The way in is a river crossing, then a long, steep bushwhack up toward the highest trees below the climb; skis help in snow. The line begins well left of the main ice, in the chimney and corner weaknesses through the lower cliff bands, and a traverse right along a large scree and snow ledge leads to the ice. Check the avalanche forecast, and treat the river crossing seriously because the ice over the river can be open.

review.notes: Approach from route page and area page; the descent is not described, so none written.

set.approach: The route starts at the foot of Triangle Falls on the north face of Triangle Peak, which stands across the North Saskatchewan River from the David Thompson Highway (Highway 11). Park on the roadside, cross the river by whatever way is safe, and bushwhack straight up toward the north face to the base of the falls. Check the avalanche forecast, and treat the river crossing seriously because the ice over the river can be open.
set.descent_text: Walk off to the west down the ridge from the top; the snow ledges may offer an escape partway up.

review.notes: Descent and start from route page (single source); approach from area page.

set.approach: The approach is the Professor Falls trail, but turn right off it before reaching the falls. Climb steep forest into the drainage below the wall, then skirt left around the cliffs until a gully leads back to the wall. Cross a bowl to a fixed rope and climb a WI3 pitch to reach the base. The wall gets no sun, and the slopes and bowl below it are avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast. The line is the right-most on the wall and starts at the Postcriptum pillar.

review.notes: Approach from area page; start from route page and Gripped; descent from route page (single source).

set.approach: The approach is the Professor Falls trail, but turn right off it before reaching the falls. Climb steep forest into the drainage below the wall, then skirt left around the cliffs until a gully leads back to the wall. Cross a bowl to a fixed rope and climb a WI3 pitch to reach the base. The wall gets no sun, and the slopes and bowl below it are avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast. From the base of the WI3 approach ice, which has a single bolt belay, continue to the start. The route sits between Sea of Vapours and The Terminator, and its first pitch begins to the right of The Replicant.

review.notes: Approach from area page and route page; descent from route page (single source).

set.approach: Park at the hot springs lot below Sulphur Mountain and follow the signed trail south down the valley. Turn right up the second obvious drainage and climb it, keeping to the right side to stay clear of the slide path where possible. If the top of the route is not in view after a short climb, you are probably in the wrong drainage. The base is under steep terrain that holds snow, so check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Approach: route page and area page parking; avalanche note from conditions page. Descent: route page only.

set.approach: From the Three Sisters Parkway exit off Highway 1, drive east to the gated boulder cul-de-sac at the road end and park. Walk east along the wide road to a fork and take the right branch into Stuart Creek, then continue up the valley, keeping right at a later fork; the path stays on the east side of the valley. Find the prominent icefall and follow scree and snow slopes up to the base. Slopes above threaten both the route and the walk in, so carry avalanche gear and check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Approach from area page and route page; no descent stated.

set.approach: Walk to Upper Twin Lake on trails from either Highway 93 South or Castle Junction. Continue along the north shore of the lake, then follow the approach route up to the base of the face. The most distinctive feature from the base is a hanging ice pitch. The face is steep, serious terrain that holds snow, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: The route ends on the ridge. From the top, scramble a short way north and make one rappel off a slung block, then follow the descent on the east ridge, traversing high toward Lower Twin Lake and meeting the lake at its north end.

review.notes: Upper Twin Lake approach and one rappel agreed by both sources; top-out gully and lake-north-end finish from Gripped only.
